newsitem.title: USA: BOXING-MOORER PLODS THROUGH DISAPPOINTING 12-ROUND TITLE DEFENSE.
newsitem.headline: BOXING-MOORER PLODS THROUGH DISAPPOINTING 12-ROUND TITLE DEFENSE.

text.p: Michael Moorer looked far from being a top heavyweight in holding onto the International Boxing Federation heavyweight title with a lackadisical majority decision win over Vaughn Bean on Saturday.
Many in the sellout crowd of 8,018 at the Las Vegas Hilton booed Moorer's plodding performance against the lightly-regarded American challenger.
"Moorer's performance was shocking," said promoter Don King.
Judge Bill Graham scored it 116-113, Jerry Roth saw it 115-113 while Dave Moretti couldn't find a winner and scored it 114-114.
"I did what I had to do. I did what I had to win," said Moorer, 39-1. "I have always had critics. Everyone is entitled to their opinion."
Not even the constant and sometimes theatrical between-rounds motivational speeches of trainer Teddy Atlas could ignite Moorer, who was a 6-to-1 betting favourite in his second title defence.
Atlas was in the face of Moorer after the very first round.
"Do not allow this guy to gain confidence," Atlas said of the 23-year-old Bean, who was rated just fifth by the IBF. "You are allowing this guy to pick his spots."

After the eighth round Atlas tried to stir up some emotion by taking out a celluar phone and telling Moorer that his son four-year-old Michael Jr. was crying in the background on the phone and wanted to know why "daddy didn't want to be world champion."
After the fight, Moorer said: "I don't think that was true. I don't even have the number where my son is right now."
Moorer was only the fifth fighter with a winning record who Bean (27-1) had fought. The combined record of his foes was an appalling 126-402-5 before the Moorer fight.
There had been enough doubt about Bean's capabilities that two members of the Nevada Athletic Commission checked out the challenger before approving the fight.
But with Moorer sleepwalking through the fight, Bean was able to put up a competitive performance.
"I felt it was a close fight, but I felt I pulled it off," said Bean.
Ageing Mexican superstar Julio Cesar Chavez held on for a closely contested unanimous decision win over Tony Martin in a non-title junior welterweight bout on the undercard.
Judges Glenn Trowbridge and two judges scored it 97-92 and Duane Ford had it 98-91.
Martin, 34-6-1, was battered, bruised and bloodied by the end of the fight.
But Chavez, 99-2-1, also looked like he had been in a fight with his face slightly disfigured and his left eye nearly closed.
"I expected him to be tough fighter," said Chavez, through an interpreter, of his American foe. "He is a very tough fighter."
The rousing 10-round war ended with both tired fighters still throwing punches in the middle of the ring.

"He's a great fighter," Martin said of the 34-year-old Chavez, a former six-time champion, who held titles in the super lightweight,junior welterweight, lightweight and super featherweight divisions. "I knew the fight was going to be a hard fight."
